hook_text: Cos of 120 degrees, no calculator, five seconds. The trick is that big angles are acute angles in costume.
clip_script: Cosine of one hundred and twenty degrees. No calculator. Five seconds. Here's the secret: every big angle is a small angle wearing a costume. Picture a bicycle wheel with one red spoke, spinning anticlockwise. Turn it to one twenty — it leans into the north-west. Now ask: what's the gap between the spoke and the horizontal line? Sixty degrees. That's the home angle — the acute angle hiding inside. The size of the answer belongs to sixty. All that's left is the sign, and the sign is pure geography. Cosine is the east-west share of the spoke. At one twenty the tip points WEST. West means negative. So cosine of one twenty is minus cosine of sixty — minus a half. Done. Sine of two hundred and ten? Home angle thirty, spoke pointing south, sine is the north-south share — minus a half. Tangent of three hundred? Home angle sixty, fourth quarter, tangent negative there — minus root three. One recipe, every time: find the home angle, read the direction, write the sign. Twelve formulae just became one drawing.
visual_style: A bicycle wheel spinning over a compass rose chalked on tar: the red spoke sweeping to 120 degrees, folding back onto 60, the west arrow glowing as a minus sign stamps onto the answer.
mood: Confident, quick, a magician revealing the mechanism.
pacing: Fast challenge open, a beat on 'costume', steady rhythm through the three worked angles.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make every reduction formula something you build, not something you memorise.
